prompt:
Return only JSON assessing this preregistered question.
Compare ALL supplied results with BOTH predictions. Cite only supplied evidence IDs.
Use survived, narrowed, rejected, or inconclusive for the working hypothesis. Empty
retrieval, failed measurements, overlapping query groups, or indistinguishable
predictions cannot establish survival. Corpus matching is exploratory and lexical;
do not claim semantic coverage or unbiased prevalence. Use signed native product,
not gate alone. Contrasts exclude common prefix tokens. Report real magnitudes only
from measurements; do not invent statistics.
Only causal_prefix (through the measured anchor) can explain that anchor's activation;
text after causal_end_char is linguistic context, never a cause of the earlier response.
Input excerpts carry original character offsets and can omit earlier context; do not
infer the absence of a contextual cue from an excerpt. Request a review if full context
is needed for a verdict. Every case's measured outcome is supplied, not just successes.
Evidence reused from the baseline and adaptively generated follow-ups are not held-out validation. RelP is attribution,
not causal proof. A suggested_revision is a proposed refinement for the next round,
not a replacement for the frozen original explanation. State unresolved limits.

claim.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with narrow unanchored-identifier suppression
claim.lede: The positive pole is driven by explicit Colorado, Denver, or Boulder entities and the local contexts they license—addresses, phone numbers, citations, datelines, state-history enumerations, and nearby spaces, punctuation, or numbers. It also fires for unambiguously Colorado local institutions and landmarks even without the word Colorado. The negative pole is sparse: mostly unanchored dense identifier blocks and one other-state “Natural Heritage” label; broad non-Colorado geography is not supported. Many no-visible-cue cases remain unresolved.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would weaken P4/P5 if known non-Colorado school districts, municipalities, or landmarks with contact blocks often fired positive, or if Colorado-specific local entities without the state word did not. I would revise N2 if dense unanchored identifiers were frequently positive outside a recognized Colorado frame, or if recognized Colorado local institutional frames still produced negative identifier blocks. I would drop N3 if other-state “Natural Heritage” labels were consistently positive. I would broaden the negative pole only if other-state administrative, legal, geographic, or natural contexts reliably and strongly predicted negative responses without Colorado cues; the measured positives among non-Colorado contexts count against that. Unexplained strong responses such as “in Bolivia” or other local-place passages remain unresolved unless a recurring contextual pattern appears.
claim.one_paragraph: Strong positive activation when the prefix names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, or Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, “at”, “is”, or following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact place tokens are strongest; weaker toponyms need an explicit Colorado frame. Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire. Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient. High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative. Inside a Colorado or known Colorado local frame—explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder, or an unambiguously Colorado school district, municipality, institution, or local-news dateline—contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: a clinic at “720-848-18…”, a school contact at “1-877-545-…”, a CSU extension URL ending “.html”, and the local-media marker “9NEWS”. The local Colorado frame must be in the prefix; a bare 720/303 number or generic contact block is not enough. Under an established Colorado frame, or when the prefix names an unambiguously Colorado local entity even without “Colorado,” weaker toponyms and nearby ordinary tokens can be positive: Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, Trail Ridge Road, High Altitude Observatory, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, Denver Broncos, Poudre School District, Broomfield, Longmont. The same word in another state, generic geology, or a broad western topic does not fire; use only with local Colorado support or an unambiguous Colorado entity.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative at the central punctuation/digit of dense identifier strings—telephone groups with parentheses or hyphens, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations of the “§ 28-33-02” type, grant IDs, and long comma-grouped area or statistical figures—when the prefix lacks any Colorado/Denver/Boulder frame or an unambiguously Colorado local entity such as Poudre School District, Broomfield, High Altitude Observatory, or Trail Ridge Road. The sign attaches to the whole formatted block, often at a space, comma, hyphen, parenthesis, or single digit. Ordinary dates, small counts, email-only contact labels, geographically nonspecific numbers, and any contact/citation inside a recognized Colorado local institutional frame are weak, unreliable, or positive under P2/P4. Negative for the capitalized label or adjacent token in an other-state natural-heritage program name such as “Alaska Natural Heritage Program” when it is outside a Colorado frame. This does not generalize to nature, wildlife, parks, outdoor recreation, rivers, mountains, or other-state geography: many such non-Colorado natural and geographical passages are positive or neutral. The cue is the program-label construction, not the topic of natural heritage.

question.question: In the positive/near-zero C1 exceptions, does the full saved context place the marked token inside a genuinely dense formatted identifier block, or is the high value attached to ordinary clinic/prose text outside such a block?
question.hypothesis: The apparent exceptions do not violate N2 because the marked token is ordinary prose or a local clinic/entity frame rather than a central punctuation/digit in a dense identifier block.
question.rival: The exceptions are genuine counterexamples: dense identifiers outside a Colorado frame can be positive, so N2 is unreliable.
question.prediction_if_hypothesis: Full contexts should show no dense phone/address/statute block at the marked token, or a positive local clinic/entity frame rather than a dense identifier.
question.prediction_if_rival: Full contexts should show a dense formatted phone/address/statute block at the marked token with positive activation.
question.distinguishing_observation: Presence or absence of a dense formatted identifier at the actual marked token in the full saved context.
question.why_new: C1 reported these as exceptions from bounded previews; it did not inspect whether the marked token itself was inside a dense block.

rows.text:
Clinics of Utah locations, we usually use conservative treatments for our patients’ bunions, although our board-certified foot surgeons can also perform surgery when necessary.
How does a bunion form?
Bunions form when there is abnormal motion and pressure across the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. This is the joint at the base of the big toe. When the normal balance of forces applied to our feet become abnormal or unbalanced, the MTP joint becomes enlarged. This forces the big toe to lean inward on the foot, and the bump forms on the inside of the foot.
Bunions are often the result of an inherited foot type that impacts the way the person walks. They can also form after a foot injury, due to certain neuromuscular disorders, or congenital deformities. People with flat feet are more prone, as are arthritis sufferers. Occupations that place inordinate amounts of stress on the feet increase the risk. Ballet dancers often develop bunions. Wearing shoes that are too tight in the toe box also contributes to bunion development.
Most bunions can be treated without surgery. These methods won’t “reverse” the bunion but can reduce pain and keep it from worsening.
- New shoes — Changing footwear is the usual first treatment approach, switching to shoes that don’t compress the toe.
- Padding — Protective pads can help cushion the painful area, but they can also increase pressure, so they may not be helpful.
- Orthotics, etc. — Orthotics (shoe inserts) can be used in your shoes, toe spacers can keep your toes apart, and a night splint can place your big toe in a straighter position.
- Icing — Icing the bunion several times a day for 20 minutes can reduce swelling.
- Medications — Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications relieve pain and reduce swelling.
If the above treatments have been used, but you’re still having problems with pain and even walking, surgery with one of our four board-certified foot surgeons could be the answer. Bunion surgery realigns bone, ligaments, tendons, and nerves so that the big toe can be brought back into the correct alignment.
If you’re dealing with the daily pain of a bunion, please give us a call at any of our five locations in American Fork (801), 763-3885; Payson, (801) 765-1718; Springville (801) 491-366

All of the earliest perissodactyls had been found in North America, dating back to around 50 million years ago. That led paleontologists to believe that the family appeared on that continent, until the discovery of Cambaytherium in 2005.
Cambaytherium was a pig-sized herbivorous animal that lived around 54.5 million years ago. It still had all five of its toes and while it may not have been an actual perissodactyl, it was probably closely related to the first true ones and can be used as a model for their appearance.
It had several features linking it to horses and rhinos, like the fused bones of its lower jaw. But it also had a suite of more primitive characteristics that make it similar to much more archaic mammals like Phenacodon, an early sheep-like creature that lived not long after the dinosaur extinction. Cambaytherium then serves as a bridge between the two families.
The remarkable thing about Cambaytherium, however, is that it was found in India, far away from North America. And at the time it lived, India was still an island slowly cruising through the Indian Ocean before eventually colliding with Asia. The finding of this transitional animal rewrote the history of how perissodactyls appeared and spread around the world.
Scientists now believe that the ancestors of Cambaytherium lived around the Arabian region and, together with other small animals like early primates and rodents, managed to access the Indian island before it actually collided with Asia. These early ungulates then used the isolated India as a haven for their evolution. When it finally integrated with the Asian continent, Cambaytherium and the first true perissodactyls could proliferate until they reached North America, where an explosion of diversity gave rise to the precursors of our familiar odd-toed ungulates.
Cambaytherium is one among many remarkable fossils that made paleontologists rethink what they knew about the history of some animal groups, and it shows us that animals that look totally different from each other today can all be descended from the same great-grandfather. In this case, it made us realize that rhinos are basically stout, rotund unicorns.
Rose, K. D.; Holbrook, L. T.; Rana, R. S.; Kumar, K.; Jones, K. E.; Ahrens, H. E.; Missia

output.result: The review hypothesis is rejected by the supplied token data. In spectrum-53716305, the peak token is the digit "0" inside the Springville phone block "(801)" with activation 4.78125; this is a genuinely dense formatted phone identifier outside any Colorado frame, not ordinary prose. The surrounding prefix includes a Utah clinic/local-location frame ("Clinics of Utah locations", American Fork, Payson, Springville), so N2 as frozen cannot dismiss it as a Colorado local institutional frame. In spectrum-95834096, the peak token is " E" in an author-initial/citation block with activation 0.02014, essentially near zero; that is not a positive dense-block counterexample, but it is also not ordinary prose. Thus C1's first exception is a real positive dense-phone case under the frozen N2 wording, while the second is near-zero in a citation/author block. N2 should be narrowed rather than treated as saved by this review; it appears to fail when a dense contact block is embedded in a non-Colorado local clinic/entity frame.
output.suggested_revision: Refine N2 for the next round: negative only for dense identifier blocks with no local clinic/entity or place frame at all; allow local institutional/place frames outside Colorado to flip contact-block signs positive. Treat author-initial/citation lists as a separate near-zero/unreliable case unless a dedicated test shows otherwise. Re-test the Utah clinic phone block as a boundary case, not as Colorado evidence.
